findings.title: Duplicate junit and hamcrest test dependencies
findings.body: The diff adds a second block declaring junit and hamcrest as test dependencies, but the original pom.xml already declares the exact same junit and hamcrest dependencies a few lines above (originally at the existing test scope block). Maven will accept this but the file now has the same dependency declared twice with identical scope, groupId, and artifactId. This is an obvious copy/paste mistake; one of the two blocks must be removed before merging.

findings.title: Dead encoder instances created and discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: In the ECDSA `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` method, the two calls `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` immediately after computing the BigIntegers create new ASN1Encoder instances, write into them, and discard the result. Only the second pair inside `writeDerSeq(...)` is actually used to build the DER output. The discarded calls are dead code (wasted allocations and a misleading read of the code) and must be removed.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK default provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns the provider that supplies the default keystore type (typically SunJCE on a standard JDK), not BouncyCastle. The interface contract and the method's name promise a BouncyCastle provider, and the existing `DefaultCryptoProvider`/`FIPS1402Provider` actually return a BC/BCFIPS instance. Any caller (now or in the future) that relies on BC-only algorithms or extensions (e.g., for `getKeyFactory`, `getSignature`, `getCertificateUtils` if they are later implemented) will silently get the JCE provider and either fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException` or produce incorrect results. The implementation must return an actual BouncyCastle provider (or the documented behaviour must be revised and the contract clarified).

findings.title: Silent behavior change when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath
findings.body: Previously `detectProvider` threw an `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found, forcing a clean classpath. The new code silently picks the highest-`order()` one and downgrades the warning to `logger.debugf`, only logging a generic "Ignored crypto providers:" message. Several built-in providers (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`) all return `order() == 200`, so when more than one is accidentally on the classpath (e.g., during testsuite setups that pull in both non-FIPS and FIPS BC) the chosen provider becomes non-deterministic and the misconfiguration is hidden from operators because the message is at DEBUG level. At a minimum the message must be emitted at WARN/INFO, and the previous hard-fail behaviour for genuinely ambiguous setups should be considered. The new `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` call also passes a pre-built string with no format specifiers to a `*f` method, which is misuse.

findings.title: readSequence can loop forever on indefinite-length encoded sequences
findings.body: `readSequence` uses `while (length > 0)` where `length` comes from `readLength()`. `readLength` returns `-1` for indefinite-length encoding (the `0x80` byte) without throwing. An indefinite-length outer sequence would therefore cause an infinite loop. ECDSA signatures use DER (no indefinite length), so this is latent, but the class is a general ASN.1 reader and this is a clear bug. Either throw on indefinite length in `readSequence` or handle it properly (look for the end-of-contents octets 0x00 0x00).

findings.title: EC key generated in constructor instead of @Before, and uses platform-default curve
findings.body: The test generates the `KeyPair` in the constructor using `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which relies on the platform-default EC parameters (P-256 on most modern JDKs but not guaranteed everywhere). The same key is then used to sign with SHA256withECDSA, SHA384withECDSA and SHA512withECDSA, producing signatures of mixed validity; the test only verifies the round-trip of the RS<->ASN1 conversion, never that the conversion matches what a real verifier would expect for ES256/ES384/ES512. Generating the key in a `@Before` method and using a deterministic curve (e.g., `ECGenParameterSpec("prime256v1")`) would make the test more reliable across JDKs and the suite more informative.

findings.title: order() added as abstract method on CryptoProvider is a breaking change
findings.body: `int order()` was added to the `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract method (not a `default`). Any external implementation of `CryptoProvider` that existed before this PR will fail to compile until it provides an implementation. This is acceptable for an internal SPI but worth noting that the order chosen (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider`=100, all built-in providers=200) makes the built-in providers always win, which is the intended behaviour but is not enforced by tests. Also consider documenting the chosen ordering semantics (higher number wins, what to choose if equal) on the interface.

findings.title: No bounds check on signature length and signLength in ECDSA converters
findings.body: `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` and `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` assume that `signature.length == signLength` and that `signLength` is even. If a caller passes a shorter signature or an odd `signLength`, the code will either throw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` from `System.arraycopy` or silently produce a truncated `s` half. A simple length check up-front would prevent surprising failures when this code is reused beyond the current authz-client wiring.
